overview.title: 📖 Overview: Coercion, Consent, and Closing a Chapter
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 21a–21b
overview.hebrewSource: חַיָּיבֵי עֲרָכִין מְמַשְׁכְּנִין אוֹתָן, חַיָּיבֵי חַטָּאוֹת וַאֲשָׁמוֹת אֵין מְמַשְׁכְּנִין אוֹתָן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf finishes the discussion of consecrating a rented house, then turns to a new mishna: when may the court repossess a debtor's property to satisfy his Temple obligations? Valuations are always collected; sin and guilt offerings never are, since the sinner needs atonement badly enough to bring them himself; burnt and peace offerings are collected, since nothing compels a person to bring them promptly. The Gemara qualifies this with exceptions and explores how a person can be 'coerced' into an offering — or a divorce — 'until he says: I want to.' It closes the chapter with a mishna opening a new topic: the public proclamation period before selling orphans' or Temple-consecrated land, and why the announcement is made both morning and evening.

slides.title: 🏠 Consecrating a Rented House
slides.subtitle: Only an owner can consecrate — so how does the baraita let a renter trigger rent payments to the Temple?

nodes.content: ❓ Baraita: 'if the one living in it consecrates it, he pays rent to the Temple.' But a renter isn't the owner!
📜 Leviticus 27:14, 'when a man shall sanctify his house' — just as a house is in one's possession, so must be anything he consecrates
💡 Resolution: read the baraita as 'if the landlord consecrates it, the renter (still living there) pays the rent to the Temple treasury'
🤔 But then the renter is misusing consecrated property (me'ila) by living there — and once he misuses it, doesn't the rent payment leave sacred status immediately?

✅ The landlord said: 'when the rent comes to me, let it be consecrated' — future proceeds, not the house itself. Rav Yehuda/Rav: this follows Rabbi Meir, who allows consecrating something 'not yet in the world'

slides.title: 💰 New Mishna: When Does the Court Repossess Property?
slides.subtitle: Not every unpaid Temple obligation is treated the same
rows: A fixed debt to the Temple treasury
Needed for atonement, so the sinner brings them without delay
Not required for atonement, so one might delay bringing them
Once his burnt/peace offering is brought he may already drink wine — risk of negligence about the sin offering
Woman after childbirth's / leper's burnt offering
Each is a prerequisite the person needs before eating sacrificial food or completing purification — no risk of delay

slides.title: 🙋 When Must the Beneficiary Consent?
slides.subtitle: Shmuel and Ulla on offerings brought by someone else on your behalf

lines.speaker: Shmuel
lines.text: A burnt offering requires the beneficiary's consent (Lev. 1:3, 'of his volition') — even when another person separates the animal for him, at the time of separation.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: A baraita: for sin/guilt offerings, consent matters only if given knowingly; for burnt/peace offerings, it works out even without consent!

lines.speaker: Shmuel
lines.text: That baraita concerns the moment of atonement (the actual sacrifice) — consent was already given earlier, at separation. That's where I require it.

lines.speaker: Ulla
lines.text: I hold the opposite emphasis: sin/guilt offerings need consent at separation; burnt/peace offerings need it only at atonement — for both pairs, atonement-stage consent is universally required.

lines.speaker: Rav Pappa
lines.text: The conflicting baraitot aren't really contradictory — one addresses the separation stage, the other the atonement stage; and Shmuel and Ulla each read the same texts in mirror-image ways.

slides.title: 🤝 Coerced 'Until He Says: I Want To'
slides.subtitle: The mishna's principle applies equally to sacrifices and to divorce

steps.content: 1️⃣ Mishna: though atonement requires bringing an offering 'of his own volition' (Lev. 1:3), the court coerces him until he says 'I want to'
2️⃣ Baraita: 'he shall sacrifice it' teaches coercion is allowed; 'of his volition' teaches it cannot be entirely forced — reconciled by coercing him until he consents verbally
3️⃣ 'And so too with bills of divorce' — the court may coerce a husband obligated by the Sages to divorce, until he says 'I want to'
4️⃣ Rav Sheshet: if a husband first files a declaration (moda'a) that any coerced get is invalid, that declaration stands — unless he later explicitly retracts it, mere compliance is not enough

slides.title: 📢 Closing the Chapter: Proclaiming a Sale
slides.subtitle: New mishna opens the topic that dominates the next several dapim
slides.label: The rule:
slides.text: The court proclaims the sale of orphans' inherited land for thirty days, and the sale of consecrated Temple property for sixty days — announcing it both morning and evening. The Gemara (Rav Yehuda, citing Rav) explains the timing: morning, when laborers head out to the fields, so an interested buyer can ask them to inspect the land for him; and evening, when laborers return to the city, reminding that same buyer to go ask them what they found.
slides.hebrewSource: שׁוּם הַיְּתוֹמִים שְׁלֹשִׁים יוֹם, וְשׁוּם הַהֶקְדֵּשׁ שִׁשִּׁים יוֹם, וּמַכְרִיזִין בַּבֹּקֶר וּבָעֶרֶב

summary.principle: Only an owner can consecrate property (though future proceeds can be pledged per Rabbi Meir); the court repossesses property for debts a person might delay (valuations, burnt/peace offerings) but not those he is desperate to pay himself (sin/guilt offerings), and it may coerce compliance — with offerings or with a get — 'until he says: I want to.'

flowSteps.content: 🏠 Only an owner can consecrate; a landlord's vow of 'future rent' works via R' Meir's rule on consecrating what doesn't yet exist
💰 Court repossesses for valuations and for burnt/peace offerings, not for sin/guilt offerings — with named exceptions each way

columns.content: 🙋 Shmuel vs. Ulla: consent for another's offering — required at separation, at atonement, or both
🤝 Coercion works 'until he says I want to' — for offerings and for divorce alike

flowSteps.content: 📢 New mishna: proclaim orphans' land sale 30 days, consecrated property 60 days, morning and evening for maximum buyer awareness
🎓 Key Principle: Jewish law coerces action but insists the person voice consent — the outward act of will still matters even under compulsion

quiz.q: How does the Gemara explain the baraita that says 'if the one living in the house consecrates it, he pays rent to the Temple,' given that only an owner can consecrate his house?
o: It means the renter secretly became the owner
It really means the landlord consecrates the house, and the renter who still lives there pays the rent to the Temple treasury
It is describing an error that the Gemara rejects entirely
It applies only to gentile renters
quiz.e: The Gemara reinterprets the baraita: the landlord (owner) consecrates, and the tenant who continues living there owes the rent to the Temple treasury instead of the landlord.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, why does the court NOT repossess property to pay for sin offerings and guilt offerings?
o: Because they are too cheap to be worth collecting
Because these offerings are needed for atonement, so a person is expected to bring them promptly without being compelled
Because sin and guilt offerings can never be brought with borrowed funds
Because they are brought only by the wealthy
quiz.e: Since a sinner needs the atonement these offerings provide, the mishna assumes he will not delay bringing them — unlike burnt and peace offerings, which are not strictly required for atonement.

quiz.q: What exception does Rav Pappa give for a case where the court DOES repossess property for a sin offering?
o: The sin offering of a leper
The sin offering of a nazirite, since once his other offerings are brought he may already drink wine, risking negligence about the sin offering
Any sin offering brought by a woman
There is no such exception
quiz.e: Rav Pappa notes that a nazirite who has brought his burnt or peace offering is already permitted to drink wine and contract impurity, creating a risk he will neglect bringing the sin offering — so the court does repossess his property for it.

quiz.q: What does Rav Sheshet rule about a husband who declares in advance (moda'a) that a bill of divorce he is about to give under coercion is invalid?
o: The declaration has no effect once he gives the get
The declaration stands and invalidates the get, unless he later explicitly retracts it
Only a court can issue such a declaration
The declaration only applies to burnt offerings, not divorce
quiz.e: Rav Sheshet teaches that a prior moda'a remains in effect even if the husband later complies and gives the get, unless he explicitly cancels the declaration — mere compliance is not treated as retraction.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara, why does the court proclaim the sale of orphans' or consecrated property specifically in the morning and in the evening?
o: Because those are the only hours courts are permitted to meet
Because those are the times laborers leave for the fields and return to the city, letting an interested buyer ask them to inspect the land and then report back
Because Temple sales require two proclamations per Torah law
Because morning and evening are when produce prices are set
quiz.e: Rav Yehuda cites Rav: the morning proclamation lets a buyer ask departing workers to examine the land, and the evening proclamation reminds him to ask the returning workers what they found.
